utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Office of the Prosecutor, Francesco Rindi, Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Jessica Lacey appearing for the Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, Aleksandar Aleksic representing Mr. Zupljanin today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I raise a few administrative matters before the witness comes. The first is this: Mr. Olmsted asked me to apply for the 92 ter package for ST-223 to be moved into evidence which he omitted to, I gather, last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the -- if it hasn't been done, then we order it to be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01744, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, the next matter is this: Mr. Zecevic, on Thursday, without notice, I gather, or just before the raised the matters, raised two matters, or, rather, three, I think, in total. One there is nothing that I need to say about it because I'm not sure what Mr. Zecevic's application was in relation to documents relating to a witness that had already testified. Second matter was in relation to disclosure which he alleged had been given to other teams which was material to this case. Namely, relating to somebody called Pecanac, I think it is pronounced. Mr. Hannis was taken by surprise. Your Honours, can I say that certainly I was aware of this disclosure. As I understood it, and we're re-checking it now, the disclosure relates to Srebrenica, disclosed in the case of Perisic and Karadzic. The majority of the documents are 95 but some are 93 and 94. Mr. Zecevic averred that there were documents that were relevant to this case, if he -- if he says he has seen the disclosure and I'm not sure how he has seen the disclosure because disclosure is supposed to be limited to each case in which it is made, and he says there are documents which are relevant then would assist us rather than having somebody to sit there to go through every single document as to which documents he says are relevant and why. So, Your Honour, that is that matter. Your Honour, we are, of course, going through it, but it will be quicker if, as I say, Mr. Zecevic tells us where those documents are. Finally, Your Honour, the question of exhumations. Yet again. Your Honour, again, and I really do say this is not a way in which matters should be gone about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner. For the continuity of the record, do you mind if I interrupt you to get response from Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, of course not, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would first like to state for the record that I informed Mr. Hannis about my intention to make the submission. And also I informed the Registry and the Court Officer about that. I also, prior to that, we filed -- we sent an e-mail requesting the Pecanac disclosure, so our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor have been notified about my submissions. Now, Your Honours, I -- I have never seen the disclosure of Pecanac. I was provided with the list of one of the Defence teams, where -- where -- where I didn't have the -- the documents but it says, for example, the document of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo, 1992. And that is how I understood that some of these documents should be -- or might be relevant to this -- to this case. That is all. I am -- I am still waiting, I officially asked the Office of the Prosecutor to give us, to provide to us the disclosure of the documents according to the Rules of the procedure. And I'm still waiting for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... still waiting because at the moment we've yet to come across a document that could be said to be relevant to this case. However, we are continuing with the search. And I don't quite understand how -- Mr. Zecevic's assertion that he hasn't seen the disclosure but he has seen a Defence document containing the disclosure. Disclosure is supposed to be confidential to each case. Your Honours, the last matter is the question of exhumations. Mr. Zecevic has gone back again over the same ground as he has gone over before. Your Honours, in addition, he tried to go back over the legal submissions when, if he gave Mr. Hannis notice, it was within a very short period of time which we argued extensively. Your Honours, we say, and I don't want to waste the Court's time by going back over it, that his quoting is selective and does not represent the position in those authorities. But in any event, Your Honours have copies of all the authorities because we referred to them in our original argument. Your Honour, can I -- can I say this: It doesn't really matter whether Mr. Zecevic stipulates to the database or not. It's Your Honours to rule on our application to add that database to our list. All the matter that Mr. Zecevic raised may go to the weight of it, but that, again, is a matter for Your Honours. It's our application which has been before Your Honours for some time now that we may add the database with the information to the 65 ter list and then have it admitted into evidence. If Your Honours give any weight to Mr. Zecevic's arguments and consider that it is incumbent on us in a case, a leadership case, to specifically prove the -- each and every entry in the database, then, of course, as I said, we'll do it. But all I'm saying, Your Honours, in which case if that is what is going to be required, then we will have to call some four or five further witnesses, at least, which will have to now be done in January, because all the witnesses -- or nearly all of them are abroad. We do urge Your Honours to make a ruling as soon as possible so that we know where we are on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. We are keenly aware of the necessity to give this matter some priority. And I can't promise a ruling before the recess, but the -- it might be possible. Thank you. Thank you. Is the Prosecution's next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And he has no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Would you be so kind as to read the solemn declaration on the card the usher has handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please be seated. And from your responses so far, I assume that you are hearing me in a language that you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we welcome you to the Tribunal, and I would point out to you that the solemn declaration that you have just made exposes to the pain of the penalties of perjury should you give false or misleading testimony to this Tribunal, which penalties this Tribunal is empowered by its constituent statute to impose. You have been called under an expedited procedure which the Rules of the Tribunal permit, and, therefore, it is expected that your testimony will be completed in the first part of today's sitting, and if I might interrupt myself for a moment, there's a question I should have asked of the Prosecution before I began. And that is, is there an indication as to how long the cross-examination of this witness would take? I don't, on the most recent information I have, have any such indication. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe not longer than one hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between half an hour and 40 minutes, which will mostly depend on the questions put by my learned friend, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, sir, you would have heard from what has just passed between the Bench and Defence counsel as to how long they expect that they would be in cross-examination. The Prosecution, at whose instance you're called, have indicated that they will spend 45 minutes in their examination-in-chief. And the practice of the Tribunal is that we sit in sessions of no longer than hour and a half, and there are two reasons for this. One is the technical necessity to change the tapes by which the proceedings of the Tribunal are recorded. And that also, secondly, allows for the convenience of yourself, counsel, and indeed the Bench but notwithstanding the set breaks that the -- that I have indicated and those breaks are of 20 minutes duration, the -- if for any reason you need to take a break before that time, if you indicate it to us we would certainly accommodate you. Would you begin by telling us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Osman Selak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is your date of birth, and what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 20th of May, 1935. I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A military officer by the rank of colonel, retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rindi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I begin my reading a short summary of the witness previous testimony in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Osman Selak, a Bosnian Muslim, was a professional soldier in the JNA from 1955 until 10 July 1992. By 1992 he had reached the rank of colonel and was in charge of logistics for the Banja Luka area of command. On 27 May 1992 Colonel Selak, participated to a meeting at the forward command post in Stara Gradiska, Croatia. Present at this meeting were, among others, Colonel Vaso Tepsic, Colonel Dragan Marcetic, and General Momir Talic. Colonel Marcetic reported that that day in Kozarac 800 people were killed and 1200 were taken prisoners. When he heard this, General Talic looked at Colonel Selak who was the only Bosnian Muslim present at the meeting and then turned to Dragan Marcetic and said, You mean that 80 persons were killed. This is the information that you're supposed to send to the General Staff. Colonel Selak later learned that there was only a little armed resistance in the Kozarac and that the real aim of the attack was to ethnically cleanse the area from non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, did you testify before this Tribunal in the Tadic case on 4 and 5 June, 1996?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: And did you testify in the Brdjanin case on 15, 16, 17, 20, 21, 23 and 24 June 2003?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Did you also testify in the Milosevic case on 12 and 13 June 2003?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: And, finally, did you testify in the Krajisnik case on 24 May 2005?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, did you have a chance to review your testimony in the Brdjanin case?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Did you review, in particular, the portions of your testimony relating to your profession background and to the attack on Kozarac at the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions on the same topic today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, I wouldn't change my answers. I would put them the same way I did then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, you testify that you had served in the JNA from 1955 to 1992. In particular, you stated that you handed over responsibilities to another officer on 10 July 1992. Did you voluntarily decide to leave the army.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain the reasons why you decided to leave the army.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I used to be a member of the JNA, which, officially, was in operation until 18 May 1992, when, in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the VRS was established. I did not wish to be a member of that army. On the 19th of May, 1992, I submitted my request for retirement, which was sent to Belgrade. The decision on retirement was made by the General Staff in Belgrade. I remained in my position until the 10th of July, 1992, when the administrative procedure was completed, and that is when I handed over my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, you told us --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Page 10, line 7, I believe the witness said, "I handed over my duties," not "my documents."

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, you told us that your ethnicity -- that you're a Bosniak by ethnicity. Did you have -- did you encounter any problem in the VRS because of your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: There were problems. Unfortunately, this also included General Adzic, who was the chief of the General Staff. At one of the meetings, he called me a Turk, whereas, I am not. General Uzelac and the corps commander -- who was the corps commander in Banja Luka and I were tasked with resolving the situation in the Krajina and he said, Uzelac, you deal with the Serbs and, Selak, you will deal with the Turks. This is why I say that he declared me a member of that community, whereas I did not feel myself to be a Turk. There were some additional problems later on, in terms of my professional duties. However, this occurred at a later stage. At any rate, it was not an easy period.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel, you said that you encountered some problems in the VRS because of your ethnicity. Did those problems influence in any way your decision to leave the army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. In February 1992, a group for co-operation with the UN was formed for the territory of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, and Serbia. I was appointed chief of that group in Banja Luka. However, the corps command sent a document to the General Staff stating that I was not to hold that position because of my political views. I was replaced on the 18th of March, not even a month after my appointment. The Tribunal has that document in its possession and I invoked that document in the Milosevic case. I don't have it with me here. It is in my hotel room if you wish to see it, but, in any case, the Tribunal has that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, in your testimony in the Brdjanin case, you described the meeting to which you participated on 27 May, 1992, in which the attack on Kozarac was discussed. You stated that you didn't know about this attack prior to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did not know about it. Although, I was commander of the logistical base which supplied all units in the area of the Bosnian Krajina, as well as the 1st and the 2nd Corps. But, however, I was completely ignorant of what was going to take place in Kozarac and Prijedor. Although, General Talic, a few days before that, had announced that he expected some problems concerning Kozarac and Prijedor. Later on, when I pondered, it became clearer to me that this had already been a preparatory stage to set the scene for the genocide that was to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: From whom did you learn the details about the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Colonel Vaso Tepic and I attended a briefing with General Talic, the corps commander, who had a forward command post in Stara Gradiska, in Croatia. Before the war, there used to be a penitentiary there. During the briefing, Colonel Dragan Marcetic was also in attendance, who was the duty officer of the head of team at the command -- at the corps command on that day. He briefed us on the events of that day in the area of responsibility of the corps. He said the following: General, today in Kozarac, 800 people were killed and 1200 were arrested. At that moment, as he was saying that, General Talic turned to me, because I was the only Bosniak there, and he reacted spontaneously in a way, because he sensed that he made a mistake looking at me. Then he turned his gaze on Mr. Marcetic and he said, I guess you're trying to say that 80 people were killed and that is what you should report to the General Staff. That particular document is also in the custody of the Tribunal. I have a copy of it as well. Unfortunately, Your Honours, far more people were killed than that. Not even today the location of the mortal remains of over 1000 people from Kozarac and Prijedor are -- they're still being looked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, you just told us that you learned that more people were killed in Kozarac as opposed to what -- what had been reported during the meeting. When was it and from whom did you learn what had really happened in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, after the 27th of May, a process of physical removal en masse began of Bosniaks and Croats from Prijedor and Kozarac. They were being transported in railway cars towards Banja Luka. Trucks were also used. People were asked for money, in order for them to be allowed to move out of Prijedor and Kozarac and to abandon their property. They had to give away their real estate. They had to sign statements to that effect --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I object. What is the point of this answer? It's not response to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, may I ask you this: From whom -- you just told us what you learned on what happened after the attack on Kozarac. From whom is it that you learned all these details?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Both during and after the war, from people who survived and who were saved because they paid to be allowed to move out of that area. They did survive but they lost many of their nearest and dearest, and they told me. Unfortunately, Your Honours, there's also a statement when 194 from -- people from Prijedor were taken by bus to Travnik to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel, Selak, may I just interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: -- for a second. You told us that you personally talked to survivors to this -- of this attack and that you learned the details from them. Did you have the chance to talk to any of your colleagues in the army about the details of this attack? And I'm referring to the period after the meeting of the 27th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to my colleagues, Colonel Tepsic, Colonel Mesud Hasotic and somebody else, but I can't remember the name now. I was in contact with the then-Major Radmilo Zeljaja, who later became lieutenant-colonel and subsequently colonel. He was directly responsible for that, and I asked him but he didn't want to reply. He just shrugged and walked away from me. He was a direct participant and the commanding officer of the then-343rd Brigade in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Besides having talked to the survivors and to your colleagues in the army about the events in Kozarac, do you remember talking to anyone else in particular about this attack?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I spoke to Muharem Krzic from Banja Luka, and the mufti, the late Effendi Halilovic. He had accurate information about what had happened. He spoke to me about it, and he communicated a lot with the people who were able to get out of Prijedor and Kozarac. There was also Mr. Adil Medic. He also lived in Banja Luka but he hails from Sanski Most. He also knows what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Could the Court Usher please display on the screen 65 ter 3644.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, could you please read to yourself the document that is displayed in front of you. And could you please let me know when you're finished reading.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I see it for the first time, Your Honours. At least I don't remember it. I reviewed a large number of documents, but I don't remember this one. However, this document is false. The information stated in it is not correct. What's contained in item 3, the total strength of the Green Berets 1500 to 2.000 men, that is wrong. I'm now speaking about Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, you just told us that the -- that this document it's wrong with regard to the number of Green Berets involved in the fighting in Kozarac. To your knowledge, how many Green Berets were involved in this -- in the fighting in Kozarac, if at all?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the notion of Green Berets is something used to denote the Army of BH. The area around Kozarac, which is in the Prijedor municipality, and in Prijedor, there was the 343rd Motorised Brigade of the JNA with over 2500 men. There was another brigade, the Kozara Brigade, and, in addition to that, there were volunteer units. If we speak about weapons held by citizens before the war the police in Prijedor had accurate information as to the type and quantity of weapons, and that is mostly hunting rifles. Supply of weapons from the outside was impossible, because from the Croatian border, all the way to Banja Luka in one direction and to Gradiska in the other, the entire territory was controlled by the JNA so it was not possible to supply the people with any weapons. So this is not correct. I'm talking -- I'm speaking now as a professional soldier. It -- what I'm saying can easily are verified because the entire area was blocked. Individuals procured weapons from Serbs because the army that was withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia distributed large quantities of weapons to the population. The word Serbian was written on houses so as to make that task easier. Thousands of pieces of weapons were distributed that way. And the Serb Democratic Party was involved, about which there's documentation here in The Hague. People bought weapons illegally from each other and from Serbs, and my personal estimate is that 50 or 70, but not more than 100 people, who had weapons. Those who had legal weapons had to return them because such was an order of the police, and who didn't return was harassed. The objective was to cleanse Kozarac fully of Bosniaks and the same applies to Prijedor and Sanski Most. The Crisis Staff of Sanski Most demanded that all Croats and Muslims leave the area, so this document is a ruse.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, could you please look at point 4, paragraph 2, of this document. It states that 80 to 100 Green Berets were killed and about 1500 were captured. Do you think that this is a truthful and accurate account of the number of person who were -- who were killed in Kozarac, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Rindi, I have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if I may, sir. Having regard to the previous answers of this witness about this document, what's the point of that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I am -- I'm trying to establish what his knowledge was of the attack in Kozarac, and he was describing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You can ask him that directly, without reference to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer the question about those killed? At the meeting with General Talic, Colonel Marcetic officially stated that 800 people had been killed on that day. The operative officer who received the report from Kozarac and this is, what does it say, 80 or something. It is obvious that this is a lie. Your Honour, I have my official notebook from that time where it says what Colonel Marcetic said officially at the meeting with General Talic; whereas this document states something different all together. It mentions 80 to 100 people. Unfortunately, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Selak, did you later learned which forces conducted the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. The 343rd Motorised Brigade participated in the attack on Kozarac, then the 6th Kozara Brigade, the volunteer units established by the Serbian Democratic Party, and the Prijedor police.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Do you know what weapons were used by the army in the attack? Do you know if heavy artillery was used during the attack, in particular?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Ground artillery was used, APCs, tanks, mortars and, naturally, all infantry weapons from machine-guns to hand-grenades and everything else. After that, the torching started, the killing and massacring of people, in which, apart from the military, the police also participated and the local Serb population too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, you mentioned the units of the army that participated to this attack. To your knowledge, were there any non-Serb officers in these units that participated to the attack?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I haven't heard of one non-Serb officer in the 343rd Brigade or in the Kozara Brigade, and there was certainly none such in the volunteer paramilitary units. So I don't know of any officer or non-commissioned officer there who was a non-Serb. That is my personal knowledge. But I believe it was the case, because they would have tried to prevent the genocide rather than take part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, for what reasons were there non-Serbs -- there were no non-Serbs in the military units that conducted this attack?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: This is an order issued by the Main Staff of the VRS that all Muslim and Croatian officers be removed from the units. I was even threatened in the newspapers and the media that I must leave the army. Therefore, it isn't logical at all. Certainly there was mistrust on the part of the Serb army toward Croats and Bosniaks, and it is only logical that there weren't any. I stand by my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, do you know what happened to the civilian population after the attack in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I do. The Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality organised the removal of all population on various grounds. It went from killings through threats and blackmail to pay with -- in cash or with jewellery. People were forced that they should renounce their real estate, and they were taken to Croatia which was closest, or on railroad carriages toward Banja Luka or on buses to Travnik. But 194 persons from those buses were killed at Koricanske Stijene, and those murders were commited by the Prijedor police which was the escort of those buses. And they were all killed, 194 persons. There were various ways, obviously, but Prijedor and Kozarac had to be cleansed. However, Sanski Most and other places in the area of responsibility of that core and the Banja Luka region were -- faired similarly and had a similar destiny.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you. You just told us that the Crisis Staff of Prijedor organised the removal of the population of Kozarac. Do you know when this removal took place?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: From May 1992 till October or November of the same year, to my mind. There were percentages stated in the official policy of the Republika Srpska that applied to the remaining shares of population groups. I'm talking about Banja Luka. Out of 50.000 Muslim and Bosniaks, only 2.000 were planned to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The witness doesn't respond to the question. That is the third or fourth time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: From whom is that you learn what happened in Kozarac after the attack?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: After the attack, apart from what was heard at the briefings of General Talic's, I heard from the Banja Luka mufti and from Muharem Krzic, Adil Medic and some other citizens from Banja Luka who had family in Prijedor because it's the neighbouring municipality. And I also heard it from other people, even Serbs who did not approve of the killing of people, their neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the houses of the inhabitants of Kozarac after the attack?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I do. No one house was left intact. There were all destroyed, burnt down, blown up. It was -- I was there in 1995 and I was appalled at what I saw there. No one house was left intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know which forces carried out this destruction of houses that you just told us about?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: It was the local Serb population. Some army members, but the police too, with the approval and the support of the police. That was the implementation of the said objective to remove all the Muslim population. It was under the control of the Crisis Staff and the members of the 343rd Motorised Brigade and paramilitary organisations but also the police from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel, based on your military knowledge, how would you describe the attack on Kozarac. Was it a small-scale attack, or was it a larger-scale attack?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Kozarac had about 4- or 5.000 inhabitants, and it was surrounded by the 343rd Brigade which was 2500 strong. There was also a TO brigade which was about 2.000 strong. There were also paramilitary formations established by the Serb Democratic Party. They were totally encircled. They couldn't leave without the knowledge and approval of those who controlled the area. Everything was blocked, roads, forests. It was impossible to leave the local commune of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: And would you describe this as a large-scale attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I object that. First of all, it is a leading question. And this witness never been in Kozarac or never spoke with anybody who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness clarified that he did speak to survivors of the attack in Kozarac. And he did also speak to colleagues or him -- of his in the army about the attack on Kozarac. Furthermore, he is a professional soldier and he's able to make an assessment as to, you know, whether or not this is a large-scale attack. He is fully competent to give an answer to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, large-scale is relative. And, so phrased, the question does appear to be leading. I suppose that a more carefully phrased question would elicit the answers that you are seeking to get, which this witness is competent to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, in military terms, how would you describe the attack against Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: As commander of the 343rd Brigade, if I had been in that position, it would have been an easy task for me because there was no resistance. There's no opposing military force that would prevent me from -- from accomplishing my mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: At what level of the military hierarchy would a decision for such an attack have to be made?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The corps commander, in agreement with the regional Crisis Staff in Banja Luka, and the Prijedor Crisis Staff, in order to implement ethnic cleansing, they would assign tasks to the army and to the civilian authorities in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: You described to us that the houses of the inhabitants of Kozarac were destroyed. Are you aware of what kind of weapons were used to destroy the houses?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of weapons were used. But it wasn't necessary to use weapons, really. There was arson, there was -- but the first thing was to loot property from the houses and then there was arson and destruction of the houses with bulldozers or any other tools. And there was -- there wasn't any need to use artillery or other weapons. The population and the police went about it, and I'm sure that members of the army and paramilitary formations also took part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You reiterated today that you testified before this Tribunal in four cases: Brdjanin, Krajisnik, Tadic, and Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Apart from that, you gave several statements to the OTP. I believe five in all. And you gave your first statement over a longer period of time from the 23rd to the 25th of September. Then, on the 30th of September, 1995; and then also from the 29th to the 31st of January, 1996, when that statement was read out to you in a language you understand and you signed it. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I know that I gave statements in that period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Following the first statement, you gave the next statement between 19th and 23rd January 2000 and the 13th of July, 2000. Next, on the 10th of March, 2001, on the 22nd of August, 2001, and the last statement was on the 22nd July, 2004. On all those occasions, the same procedure was followed. That is to say, once the taking of the statement was completed, the translator would put it in your language, whereupon you would sign, affirming that the statement in question contains everything you have said to the best of your recollection; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, during the proofing for the Brdjanin case, as well as the Krajisnik case, you had occasion to see the statements and offer amendments or corrections caused by typographical errors.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I remember the discussions, but I don't know whether I made any corrections and changes because it's been a while. In any case, my signature is there, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: As regards the meeting at the forward command post, that day you went to Gradiska to attend a briefing, together with Colonel Tepsic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And I suppose you returned to Banja Luka the same day or the next.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: We returned on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You said that, in addition to Colonel Tepsic, you discussed these events with Colonel Hasotic as well, if I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Mesud Hasotic, who was the assistant commander for morale in the Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hasotic was in Banja Luka at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: He was in the corps command. He was the assistant to the chief -- sorry. Assistant to the commander of the corps in charge of morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You were just shown a combat report sent by the corps to the Main Staff, and you said that you see that document for the first time. You will -- have also stated your opinion. However, as the logistics base commander, you did not take part in the drafting of corps reports that were to be sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, I was not part of the corps. I was directly under the command of the Main Staff. The corps command sent their own reports; whereas, I sent my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That means that you did not personally participate in the drafting of combat documents of the corps, such as orders and like.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Today you also said -- sorry. First of all, tell me this. Do you know whether Colonels Tepsic and Marcetic are still alive?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Colonel Tepsic was killed in a car accident during the war. Colonel Marcetic, as far as I know, is alive. However, we haven't been in contact for over ten years, so I have no reliable information on him, and I don't know of his whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You also stated today that you discussed these events with Mr. Krzic as well as the mufti, Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And the two of them were both in Banja Luka at the time. They resided there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Krzic, however was often on the move, but he did live in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And you said that -- well, you didn't say that, but Mr. Krzic was a president of one of SDA boards in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: He was a member, although I don't know his position. I was never a member of any party. I only know that he was a member of that party but I don't know what his position within it was. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Neither yourself not your colleagues, Colonel Tepsic; Hasotic; Marcetic; nor Mr. Krzic; the mufti, Halilovic, none of these that you discussed these events with at the time was in Kozarac at the time, in the course of those few days?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Everyone except Colonel Marcetic, who was in the corps command as operations officer had no knowledge about that. Only he could know about it. He must have been present there, because he was also in charge of planning operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: At the briefing of the 27th of May at the forward command post, did you report to anyone along your professional line? Did you report this to any of your superiors about what you heard?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I didn't report this officially to anyone because I was subordinated to the Main Staff of the VRS. They received their corps report. Hence, there was no need for me to report anything to any of my superiors and I did not, at least not in official terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 65 ter document 09135 which is tab 1 of the Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I have a hard copy for you as well. That is the first statement you provided, and I'm interested in a single paragraph. On page 9 in the English; in the B/C/S, it is at the bottom of page 10 and at the top of page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English, it's page 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said page 10 for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The end of page 2 [as interpreted], the beginning of page 11 for you. For the Judges and others who follow it in English, page 10; page 9 in e-court. On the last page 10 and on page 11 you say, among other things: "It was possible that the 343rd Brigade drafted all of the plans which were then submitted for approval to the corps commander. In that case, General Talic only had to call General Arsic and tell him that the plan was approved. In the attack on Kozarac, the 343rd Brigade took part." And, as you said, it was 3- to 3.500 soldiers strong, two TO units previously mobilised and attached to the 343rd Brigade, as well as some paramilitary units. In terms of the amount of ammunition kept on hand by units, the corps carries with it three combat sets. This is your explanation of the amount of ammunition. Do you recall having given this statement in 1995 and early 1996. You also signed it, most likely, before you appeared here for the first time in the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see a problem here. The 343rd Motorised Brigade was one of the strongest brigades in the Banja Luka Corps. The TO brigade units at Kozara that were mobilised participated as well as the paramilitary or volunteer units established by the SDS, comprising Serbs from that area. I don't see what the point in question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And you stand by the statement you provided then in 1995 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I do. There's one thing I would like to add, Your Honours. The plan of operations as well as the orders arrived from the corps command, and the brigade implemented them, and other units, save for the brigade. There were other units taking part as well. The brigade itself and its commander could not attack or engage a single position without an approval or knowledge by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Based on your military experience, you drew that conclusion, as things should have been, but regarding this event, you were not familiar with any ideas of Colonel Arsic and you did not see any orders or approvals by the corps commander. You did not see any of those?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I did not. But the corps commander would be held responsible if he did anything without the knowledge or approval of the corps commander. The goal was clear, which was to -- to ethnically cleanse Prijedor and Kozarac of Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you know that a few days before the event in Kozarac, there was an incident when a military column was attacked? First, there was an incident in Hambarine, and a day or two later in Jakupovici, the JNA column was attacked.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I do know about that. I know that a soldier was killed. But an incident can take place even between people manning check-points because there were barricades on the road. People were quite upset, angered. They were not allowed to move freely or to travel, and in such a situation, incidents can occur. However, that is no excuse for killing a few thousands people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have one clarification question. On page 27, line 18, the witness answers: "The corps commander would be held responsible if he did anything without the knowledge or approval of the corps commander." That's obviously a mistake and I suppose the witness has said something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The brigade commander. If he would dare do anything without the knowledge of the corps commander. I may have misspoken. In any case, the commander of the 343rd Brigade was Mr. Arsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, before you were retired, you had a career with the JNA spanning over 40 years; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. I began working in 1958 after having received my university degree in Zagreb. I submitted my request in 1952, which makes me 37 at the time, and I had some modest previous experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D0-0471 [as interpreted], tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just have a small correction to the transcript. It says at line 28 -- sorry, page 28, line 24, I submitted my request in 1952. I believe there might be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. 1992. 19th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked for the -- for the document 1D04-4771. It's tab number 5 of the Defence [indiscernible] documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this is a decision on your retirement dated 7 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this concern you personally?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom it says that he was relieved of military service on the 30th of September 1992 by decision of the appropriate officer. Then it says according to the data registered in personnel records, he has 40 years, eight months and three days of employment.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please allow me to put my question first. When I mentioned the 40 years, I meant to say that you, as an active-duty officer, had an accelerated employment history in the way you gathered your experience and years of service.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. But not active duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have interpreters here; hence, I'd like to ask you to pause before answering so that we would have my question and your answer recorded correctly. For every year of service as an active-duty officer, instead of 12 months, you received more credit; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, in the JNA, officers and non-commissioned officers in command positions had accelerated length of service up to three months. Command officers, military educational institutions, and commands starting from the level of corps and up, did not have accelerated length of service. I worked at the Military Academy in Banja Luka for over 15 years, and I had no accelerated service because I was in the technical department. The commanding personnel, COs and NCOs, had accelerated length of service. I did not, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, during at least a leg of your career, you did enjoy the status of having an accelerated length of service awarded; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there's no objection, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But I thought this witness explained that he didn't fall in this category.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, my first question was that -- does he recognise this as his retirement -- decision on his retirement and he said yes. That's my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D00400. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, during your career, you were in various positions, as you told us, in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, which positions did you hold in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I was commander of the logistics base in Banja Luka. In the 993rd Logistics Base in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's the same position which you occupied until your retirement in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from one month when I was chief of group for co-operation with the UN forces, but then I was removed from that position for political -- because I was up -- I was politically not apt unfit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in 1991, and during the conflicts in the territory of Croatia, that logistics base commanded by you had a certain role to play in that; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. It provided logistics support to the units of the 5th Krajina Corps, the 50th Partisan Division, and all units in the area of Bosanska Krajina and some parts of Croatia, across the river Sava, that took part in the combat operations in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'll show you a document, 1D04-4814, which is under tab 16. 4814. Sir, this is a proposal put to the Federal Secretary of National Defence, which says: For exceptional services rendered to the armed forces of the SFRY, for the competence and courage in command and control of units during wartime assignments, we recommend the following active duty military personnel be awarded some decorations. And you are mentioned under (b) 2 to be decorated with the order of the People's Army with a laurel wreath; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this applies to you, this proposal?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, your superiors at that time were more than satisfied with the way you carried out your tasks and felt that you carried them out excellently and that's why they are proposing that you be decorated; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document is dated 3 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. But the proposal was not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But your commander Colonel-General Nikola Uzelac made the proposal?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: He was not my commander. I was subordinated to the command of the army and not to the command of the corps. I know of this proposal, but it was not accepted. I don't know for which reasons, maybe because subsequently the situation changed completely. However, I was not decorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To what end, Mr. Zecevic? Is the proposal that he be decorated and he was not? We have his answer on it's record. Do we need the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you move on, it seems to be a convenient point to take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RINDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio joined the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rindi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, since you were commander of the logistics base, I suppose that you're familiar with the decision or the order of the Presidency of the SFRY from the end of 1990 about the removal of equipment and weapons from the warehouses of the TO.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That order was adopted by the Presidency of the SFRY and since the TO of every republic was subordinate to the Presidency of that respective republic, the Presidencies of these republics adopted a similar decision that applied to the territory of that particular republic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That decision about the removal of weapons and equipment from the warehouses of the TO was applied in the entire territory of the SFRY; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us show the witness 1D04-4791, please. It's under tab 11. While we wait, sir, do you know that the decision was applied in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. I did not have the document, but I had information that it was applied. I have no documents that corroborate this statement. I believe it was applied. Whether it was applied entirely, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the reply of the Ministry of Defence to a question asked by one of the deputies in the Republican Assembly of Serbia of 26 February 1991 and the question was about the removal of weapons and equipment. And the then-minister of National Defence in the cabinet of the Republic of Serbia 1991, vice-admiral, Miodrag Jokic, drafted the reply of the Ministry of Defence and says: The decision of -- to remove weapons and equipment from the warehouses of the Territorial Defence was adopted for -- exclusively for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I do not see that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is on page 3, but I suppose you didn't have a chance to see the document before coming here?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm reading it out to you. Whether the justification for the decision of the Presidency of the SFRY were security considerations.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I say "decision," I mean the decision to remove weapons and military gear from the warehouses of the TO and other entities in the system of the -- of All People's Defence and social self-protection. The reasons for the decision on that removal were security considerations; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. Can I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do it briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The reason was to take away weapons from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, and Slovenia because the political situation in Yugoslavia was such that a breakup was expected: The breakup of Yugoslavia. That's why weapons were taken away from the TO, in order to make it impossible for the republics of Slovenia Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina to defend themselves in -- if there should be the need to do so. But the reason was not the security of Yugoslavia. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But we see here that the same was done in Serbia, in the Socialist Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. But the weapons were returned to the warehouses of the logistics bases of the JNA, and the JNA later on distributed these weapons only to the Serb people when Yugoslavia began to break up. And that's -- that was the reason why this was decided to make it impossible for these three peoples to come by weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please limit yourself to answering my questions and do not volunteer any comments. You will have the opportunity to make comments. I asked you whether it was enforce in the territories of SFRY. You said yes. And I showed you a document that it was also done in the Socialist Republic of Serbia. Then you said that these weapons were transferred to the logistics bases of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this transfer of weapons in the entire territory of the SFRY from the warehouses to the -- of the TO to the logistics bases of the JNA was carried out wherever that order was carried out; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Here's my question: The weapons and military gear that were removed from the warehouses of the TO, were they put in the warehouses and the bases of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness 1D04-4778, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Last two digits 98. It's tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the decision to remove weapons and military gear from the warehouses of the TO and the placing of the same in the warehouses of the JNA were -- were a decision of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We see that it is confirmed in this document which is an order signed by Colonel-General Milos Bajcetic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, I have the document myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this the document?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us sum up. The Presidency of the SFRY took this decision at the federal and at the level of the -- of -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of BH issued the same order and we can see it now in front of us.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this Milos Bajcetic, what did he command, the TO?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose whereas it -- it appears somewhat illogical as going in through this witness. Inasmuch as he challenges the contents, there's no -- the relevance of it, in the context of his evidence, is obvious. Is that your position, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is my position, Your Honours, and I don't think that -- that he challenges the contents of it. He confirms all the contents and says he has this same order and it was -- it was signed by the commander of the TO at the time of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps I misspoke when I said he challenged the contents. But he challenges the operation. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D00401, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, tell me, in the area of responsibility of a military unit, the commander of that unit also issues permits to persons who are not members of that unit to be allowed to move about.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of a military unit, the commander of that unit, among others, also issues permits to individuals in that area to move about.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us show the witness 1D04-4801. Tab 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we go on, I just want to point out at page 37, line 10, the -- what is attributed to Mr. Zecevic about the -- in response to his application to tender document was a comment that I would have made. Yes, Mr. Zecevic, please continue [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a document here and that is why I asked you, it's dated the 26th June 1992. It's a permit. And we see in the signature block Major-General Momir Talic and it's a permit issued to a person or a delegation to travel along the Doboj-Prnjavor-Banja Luka route. It's a delegation that comprised of nine persons and I believe that this document was shown to you in the Brdjanin trial?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: This is about an official delegation. You asked me about individuals but a corps commander has no need to do that. However, in a zone of combat operations where there is military activity, it is normal for such permits to be issued, but only in zones of combat operations, not elsewhere, and for -- for the purpose of prospecting human lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. I made a mistake. I should have been more specific and mentioned zones of combat operations. I merely mentioned the areas of responsibilities of military units. Thank you, sir. Sir, you mentioned the assistant commander for moral education and propaganda activity, Colonel Hasotic, who worked in the 5th Corps command, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I show you a document dated 21 April 1992, signed by Mr. -- or, rather, Colonel Hasotic. And 1D04-4765, tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us show page 3 to the witness so he may see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the signature, assistant commander for MV and PP, Colonel Mesud Hasotic. Do you recognise the signature of Mr. Hasotic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise the signature but I know about this document, and I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is -- this information is dated 21 April which we will see if we go back to page 1. It is meant to inform the command of the 2nd Military District about the situations in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And on page 2, some incidents are mentioned. You said that you have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that there's a mention made of an attack by the Red Berets and MUP special forces on the Pretis factory in Vogosca between the 17th and 18th of April during the night? Next there was an attack on the military factory at Igman on the same date. Do you recall that? And it goes on.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I do recall that. Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put the question first: Colonel Mesud Hasotic is a Bosniak, is he not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In response to my learned friend's question, you discussed your position as a member of different community or ethnicity while you were a member of the VRS until you were retired. Do you recall having discussed this with my learned friend?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At page 3, item 5, signed by Mr. Mesud Hasotic, there is something I wanted to show you. It has to do with the situation in which the Muslim and Croatian active servicemen and civilians employed in the JNA have found themselves in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He states that they are treated the same as everyone else. Their status has not changed. And he also states that those who stayed make us especially happy and that is the way they should be treated in all subordinated commands and units.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, can I see that. But could we please go to page 1 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to page 1 for the sake of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document only conveys information of the 2nd Military District command. It wasn't drafted by Colonel Hasotic. He is simply passing on information. He copied it. He was obliged to do so as a corps member in order to forward that information to the corps subordinate units. This is not his document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were directly subordinated to the Military District Command.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, the 2nd Military District of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you were not directly subordinated to the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So your directly superior command was the command of the 2nd Military District. And you assert that what the assistant commander of the corps, Mr. Hasotic, is conveying in his dispatch is untrue. Is this what you say?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that this was not his document. He merely passed it on to the corps subordinate units, and he signed it as the person who had that obligation. And he specifically says, We hereby forward to you the information of the command of the 2nd Military District. The first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I believe it is not in dispute that in the armed forces hierarchy is of utmost importance.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise, it wouldn't function properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, the command of the 2nd District which was your directly superior command, as it was in the case of the 5th Corps as well, asserted this. Mr. Hasotic conveyed that information to the 5th Corps subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you are trying to tell us that -- you are trying to tell us that what your superior command of the Military District stated in the document is untrue.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I'm not saying it is not true. Parts of it were not true because the JNA, at the time, was against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was in favour of creating the -- a Greater Serbia. It sided with only one people, and it was no longer Yugoslav. It was a Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I specifically asked you about item 5. We read it together and we commented upon it. Are you stating that the Military District Command stated something that was untrue in passing this information on to the corps and its subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, I assert that it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Given your long experience in the JNA, is it not a fact that it is of essential importance to report precisely?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. There was such an obligation, and one could be held accountable for providing inaccurate or untrue information. There would be disciplinary measures taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at the beginning of today's hearing, with my learned friend, you discussed your duties as commander of the logistics base. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood properly, as the commander, you provided supplies for all units in the Bosanska Krajina. You supplied weapons, equipment, ammunition, et cetera; correct? It all came from your base.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, to all JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And when, on the 19th of May, the JNA withdrew --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: On the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When, on the 18th of May, the JNA withdrew from Bosnia and Herzegovina and when the VRS was formed, that logistics base continued supplying equipment, weapons, and ammunition to the units of the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must respond to this. The JNA did not withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was simply renamed. Instead of the JNA, it was called VRS. All of the units that had been in that area were simply renamed. My base was too. My base too was renamed to become the 14th Logistics Base instead of the 993rd. Not a single unit withdraw. Actually, it was the units from Slovenia and Croatia which had withdrawn and came to Bosnia-Herzegovina were renamed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours are on this. Your Honour, I don't see what any of this has got to with the adjudicated fact about which this witness has been called to testify. Your Honours have very strictly limited what we can lead from witnesses to the adjudicated fact, and while I appreciate that cross-examination may go further, this is miles from anything to do with Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I totally disagree and if my learned friend will have a bit of patience, my next question will very clearly establish the connection between my first question and the -- the actual adjudicated fact that this witness is -- is coming to testify. Your Honours, I cannot be held responsible for witness giving the answers way beyond what was the scope of the question. I just want to interrupt him because I guess it is not looked favourably by the Trial Chamber to interrupt the witness. That is why -- that is the only reason why I don't interrupt the witness, otherwise I would have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, this has been going for some time because documents have been put to him too, we would suggest have very little to do with it. But I'm merely mentioning it, Your Honours. And if Your Honours feel it's relevant then I won't take it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Zecevic, you would move rapidly to your question that links it to the adjudicated fact which the witness is here to testify to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, for any larger scale operation or offensive in the territory of Bosanska Krajina, you, as the logistics base commander in charge of supplying weapons and ammunition, must have been informed of those; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I should have been, but I was summoned to attend such meetings when plans were made half an hour later, precisely so that I wouldn't know exactly what was being planned and I mean the meetings with General Uzelac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of the fact whether you were called to the meetings or not, even if you were called to a meeting without a written order, I presume you would not have allowed any equipment, ammunition or weapons to leave your logistics base?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, for any larger scale operation, you received a written order to supply a quantity of ammunition, military equipment, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Because the corps had three combat ammunition and fuel kits which were there to satisfy any operation between five and ten days. I wasn't privy to it -- individual requests. We only reacted to such wholesale requests, as a base.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on two occasions, you discussed a meeting, that was during examination-in-chief and during cross-examination of Mr. Aleksic, you discussed the meeting of the 27th of May with General Talic. Apologies. Your answer was not recorded. Please pause. Please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I said this: On two occasions today, you responded to both the Prosecution and Defence about questions on the meeting of the 27th of May, 1992, and your answer was affirmative in both instances.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, that meeting was actually a daily briefing, was it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: It was a briefing with the corps commander, which I attended as the base commander, in order to receive information on the logistical needs of the corps so as to shorten the time needed for passing that information through the pipeline. That's why I was called to such briefings as that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And such briefings took place daily with the corps commander, irrespective of whether you were called to them or not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That daily briefing was chaired by Colonel Marcetic.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. Colonel Marcetic was the head of the management team which received information from subordinate units and he passed the commander's orders to those units. Such chiefs changed daily. They were in charge of receiving and passing on information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear this up. The management team was part of the corps command, and each day another officer was in charge of it, for that day.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. The title was the chief of the management or control team for a particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that chief, as well as the team itself, received information from the field and informed the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Not from the field. From the subordinate units. We need to be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I said "from the field," that what's I meant, the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The field is one thing. The units are -- is another. He received unit reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, all information provided by Mr. Marcetic about the events in Kozarac is information he had received, I suppose, from the command of the 343rd Motorised Brigade from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In its daily report, the 343rd Brigade reported to the corps about the attack in the area of the village of Kozarac on the 27th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I suppose it was so. Although he did not mention the establishment of the camps of Keraterm and Omarska, because they were formed at that very same time, and they had over 5.000 inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The gist of it is, that Colonel Marcetic conveyed information to you and to the command which he had received from a subordinate unit.
